newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Germans, French play down differences over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Germans, French play down differences over EMU.

text.p: German and French officials sought at the Davos summit to defuse a row over the European central bank's independence and said it would be immune from political pressure when the single currency starts in 1999.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel went so far as to say he favoured a French proposal for an informal "stability council" to coordinate policy among member governments after the launch of a single European currency.

"This kind of body makes sense for countries in the third stage of Economic and Currency Union (EMU)," Waigel told reporters at the annual World Economic Forum in Davos, referring to the launch of a single currency.

"A stability council would be an informal body with no decision-making power," Waigel added, making clear the panel could not act as a pro-growth political counterweight to central bankers intent on keeping inflation under control.

The proposal has come under fire from Germany's Bundesbank, which fears it might be used to undermine the independence of the European Central Bank (ECB) that is due to start work with the launch of the single currency.
But Waigel said the independence of the ECB was guaranteed by the Maastricht Treaty.

"The independence of the European Central Bank is made even clearer in the Maastricht Treaty than (the Bundesbank's independence) in the German central bank law, and it wll stay that way," Waigel said.

Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet said the stability council would coordinate policy among governments taking part in the single currency and look after implementation of a budget discipline pact agreed at an EU summit in December.

"The council of stability is a way that the French government has entertained to be sure that the implementation of this stability pact will be good, and as good as possible," Trichet told Reuters Financial Television in Davos.
"The independence of the central bank is enshrined in the (Maastricht) treaty and there is absolutely no point that this independence could be hampered in any respect," he added.

Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, vice president of Germany's powerful central bank, said he had no doubt that France would respect the future central bank's independence, even though some people in France questioned this.
"But what is decisive is what the French political leadership thinks, and here I have no doubt that it backs the compromises found in the Maastricht Treaty," he said.
European Commission President Jacques Santer told politicians to keep their hands off the euro and leave monetary policy to the European Union's central bank.
"We on the Commission are of the opinion that we should implement the Maastricht Treaty as is," Santer told reporters at the annual gathering of business and political leaders.
He said the EU executive would not take a formal position on the French suggestion because it went beyond the 1991 treaty.

"But in my personal opinion the stability council cannot be allowed to affect the independent status of the European Central Bank," he said. "And secondly it can have only an informal character because it is not envisioned in the Treaty."
Santer said it was time to stop debating whether politicians should have a big say in monetary policy once the single currency, which he called "irreversible", arrives in 1999.
"I think it would be useful at this time if one would not enter into further debate about the position of the European Central Bank," he said.
"The position of the European Central Bank is clearly defined in the Maastricht Treaty and one may not upset it."
He insisted that strict financial criteria in the treaty would be applied when judging next year which countries qualify for the project on the basis on their 1997 economic performance.

"We are sticking to the tight criteria of Maastricht. There will be no flexibility in this respect," he said, singling out the public-sector deficit ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product for special mention.
